title: More practice · B2
desc: Extra exercises for each B2 unit.
intro: One topic for each part of the unit. Each practice brings ALL the exercises of the topic: first the ones you got wrong, then the new ones.

sets.title: Relative clauses and reduced clauses
sets.intro: Relative clauses add information about a noun. Non-defining clauses use commas, and you can shorten many clauses with -ing or -ed.

watch.wrong: My sister, that lives in Monterrey, is a nurse.
watch.right: My sister, who lives in Monterrey, is a nurse.
watch.why: Between commas, do not use that.

watch.wrong: The pizza that I ate it was cold.
watch.right: The pizza that I ate was cold.
watch.why: Do not repeat the object pronoun.

watch.wrong: The woman talked to me is my aunt.
watch.right: The woman talking to me is my aunt.

items.prompt: My uncle, ___ lives in Chicago, is a chef.
items.explain: In a non-defining clause about a person, use who (not that).

items.prompt: The neighbors ___ dog barks all night are moving out.
That is the school ___ my parents first met.
He forgot my birthday again, ___ really upset me.
items.explain: Which can refer to a whole idea.

items.prompt: The woman ___ at the next table is my old teacher. (sit, reduced clause)
items.explain: Active meaning: reduce the clause with -ing.

items.prompt: Emails ___ after midnight are usually ignored. (send, reduced clause)
items.explain: Passive meaning: reduce the clause with a past participle.

items.prompt: The hotel in ___ we stayed was spotless. (preposition + pronoun)
items.explain: After a preposition, use which for things.

items.prompt: The colleague with ___ I share an office is very quiet. (formal)
items.explain: After a preposition, use whom for people in formal English.

items.prompt: Passengers ___ luggage is overweight must pay extra.
items.explain: Whose + noun shows that the noun belongs to the person.

items.prompt: I remember the summer ___ we drove across the country.
items.explain: When can follow a time noun.

items.prompt: The documents ___ by the lawyer were incomplete. (prepare, reduced clause)
Anyone ___ to join the club should email me. (want, reduced clause)
My brother, ___ is a nurse, works nights.
items.explain: Use who between commas, not that.

items.prompt: Is this the town ___ you grew up?
My cousin, ___, just got engaged.
items.explain: Non-defining clauses use who for people and never that.

items.prompt: The man ___ is my boss.
items.explain: An active action in progress is reduced with -ing.

items.prompt: I have a friend ___ mother is a pilot.
She passed the exam, ___ surprised everyone.
items.explain: Which can refer to the whole previous idea.

items.prompt: The house ___ I grew up is now a museum.
Which sentence is correct?
options: The girl who I met her is kind.
The girl I met is kind.
The girl I met her is kind.
The girl whom I met her is kind.
items.explain: Do not repeat the object pronoun inside the clause.

items.prompt: My sister, that lives in Lima, is a dentist.
answers: My sister, who lives in Lima, is a dentist.
items.explain: Non-defining clauses do not use that.

items.prompt: The book which I bought it was boring.
answers: The book which I bought was boring.
The book I bought was boring.
The book that I bought was boring.
items.explain: Do not repeat the object after the verb.

items.prompt: I know a man which daughter is an astronaut.
answers: I know a man whose daughter is an astronaut.

items.prompt: The teacher with who I studied retired.
answers: The teacher with whom I studied retired.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: The man standing at the door is my landlord
items.explain: A reduced -ing clause follows the noun.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: My boss whose car was stolen called the police
items.explain: Whose connects the person and the possession.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: Mia lost her keys which made her late
items.explain: Which refers to the whole idea.

items.prompt: Mi hermano, que vive en Madrid, trabaja en un banco.
answers: My brother, who lives in Madrid, works at a bank.

items.prompt: La casa donde crecí fue vendida.
answers: The house where I grew up was sold.
The house I grew up in was sold.
The house that I grew up in was sold.
The house in which I grew up was sold.
items.explain: Where can replace a preposition + which.

items.prompt: Conozco a una chica cuyo papá es piloto.
answers: I know a girl whose dad is a pilot.
I know a girl whose father is a pilot.

sets.title: Character and the circle of friends
sets.intro: Use these adjectives and nouns to describe people and how close you are to them.

learn.def: a person you know a little, but not well
learn.example: I only know her as an acquaintance from my yoga class.

learn.def: with strong, warm relationships
learn.example: We grew up in a small, close-knit community.

learn.def: a person you trust with your secrets
learn.example: Pedro is my confidant; I tell him everything.

learn.def: always faithful to your friends or team
learn.example: A loyal friend defends you when you are not there.

learn.def: honest and safe to rely on
learn.example: Never lend money to someone who isn't trustworthy.

learn.def: relaxed and not easily upset
learn.example: Rafa is so easygoing that nothing stresses him.

learn.def: too interested in other people's business
learn.example: Our nosy neighbor asks about my salary.

learn.def: wanting someone all for yourself
learn.example: Tom is too possessive to let his girlfriend go out alone.

learn.def: quiet and private about your feelings
learn.example: Lena is reserved with new people.

learn.def: often changing from happy to angry without warning
learn.example: He is so moody that I never know what to expect.

learn.def: friendly and fond of being with others
learn.example: Gabriel is sociable and loves big parties.

learn.def: a friend that two people both have
learn.example: We met through a mutual friend.

items.prompt: I only know her a little. She is an ___ from my English class.
items.explain: An acquaintance is someone you know a little.

items.prompt: Our family is very ___: we eat together every Sunday and support each other.
You can tell Pedro your secrets. He is a real ___ and never repeats anything. (a person you trust with private things)
Dana always keeps her promises and defends her friends, so she is very ___.
Don't leave your wallet with anyone who isn't ___. (honest and reliable)
items.explain: Trustworthy means you can rely on the person.

items.prompt: Rafa never gets angry about small things. He is so ___.
My neighbor asks about my salary and my love life. He is so ___! (too curious about others)
items.explain: Nosy people ask too many personal questions.

items.prompt: Tom doesn't like sharing his girlfriend's time with anyone. He is too ___. (wants her only for himself)
items.explain: Possessive means wanting to control someone.

items.prompt: Lena doesn't talk much with new people. She is quite ___. (quiet and private)
items.explain: Reserved people keep their feelings private.

items.prompt: One minute he is laughing, the next he is angry. He is so ___. (his mood changes quickly)
Gabriel loves parties and meeting new people. He is very ___. (friendly, enjoys company)
items.explain: Sociable people enjoy being with others.

items.prompt: We have a ___ friend: she introduced us last year. (a friend that both of us have)
items.explain: A mutual friend is shared by two people.

items.prompt: A ___ customer buys from the same shop for years, even when it is more expensive.
items.explain: Loyal also describes customers and fans.

items.prompt: We grew up in a small, ___ town where everybody helps everybody.
items.explain: Close-knit describes groups with strong ties.

items.prompt: A confidant is someone who...
items.explain: A confidant is a trusted listener.

items.prompt: Which word describes a person who asks too many personal questions?
Which is the opposite of sociable?
items.explain: A reserved person prefers to keep to themselves.

items.prompt: Eva gets upset if her partner has plans without her. She is...
items.explain: Possessive means wanting someone all for yourself.

items.prompt: 'We have a mutual friend' means...
options: We both know the same friend.

items.prompt: He keeps his promises and you can believe him. He is...
He is a very easygoing, so nothing upsets him.
answers: He is very easygoing, so nothing upsets him.
items.explain: Do not use a before very + adjective.

items.prompt: We have a common friend called Leo, and we both love him.
answers: We have a mutual friend called Leo, and we both love him.
items.explain: In this meaning English uses mutual friend.

items.prompt: He is reserved, so he talks to every stranger at parties.
answers: He is sociable, so he talks to every stranger at parties.
He is reserved, so he never talks to strangers at parties.
items.explain: Reserved and talking to every stranger do not match.

items.prompt: Our family is very close knitted.
answers: Our family is very close knit.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: She is a loyal friend who never lets me down

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: Nobody tells Dan secrets because he is so nosy

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: He is too possessive to share his time

items.prompt: Mi cuñado es muy despreocupado y nunca se enoja.
answers: My brother-in-law is very easygoing and never gets angry.
My brother-in-law is very easygoing and never gets mad.

items.prompt: Ella es una conocida, no una amiga.
answers: She is an acquaintance, not a friend.
She's an acquaintance, not a friend.
items.explain: An acquaintance is not a close friend.

items.prompt: Tenemos un amigo en común.
answers: We have a friend in common.

sets.title: Phrasal verbs for relationships
sets.intro: Phrasal verbs are everywhere when we talk about friends, family and couples. Learn each one inside a sentence.

learn.def: to stop being friends after an argument
learn.example: Tom fell out with his cousin over a loan.

learn.def: to become friends again after an argument
learn.example: We made up with each other the next day.

learn.def: to slowly become less close
learn.example: They drifted apart after college.

learn.def: to stop communicating with someone
learn.example: I lost touch with my first boss.

learn.def: to continue to communicate
learn.example: Keep in touch while you are abroad.

learn.def: to have a good relationship with
learn.example: She gets along with all her coworkers.

learn.def: to admire and respect
learn.example: I look up to my grandmother.

learn.def: to disappoint by not doing what you promised
learn.example: Please don't let me down this time.

learn.def: to depend on
learn.example: You can count on me.

learn.def: to end a romantic relationship
learn.example: He broke up with her by text.

learn.def: to start a stable life in one place
learn.example: They want to settle down and have kids.

learn.def: to accept something annoying
learn.example: I can't put up with his late replies.

items.prompt: Tom and I ___ over money last year, and we still don't speak. (fall out)
items.explain: Fall out is irregular: fell out.

items.prompt: Let's stop arguing and ___! (make up)
They were close at school, but they ___ after moving to different cities. (drift apart)
I ___ touch with my old classmates when I changed phones. (lose)
items.explain: Lose touch: lost in the past.

items.prompt: Please ___ in touch while you are traveling. (keep)
items.explain: Keep in touch = continue to communicate.

items.prompt: I get ___ with my in-laws, and we never argue.
items.explain: Get along with = have a good relationship.

items.prompt: She really ___ her grandmother, who raised five children alone. (look up to)
Don't worry, you can ___ on me. I'll be there. (count)
My manager never ___ me down; she always keeps her word. (let)
items.explain: Let down = disappoint; the verb takes -s.

items.prompt: She decided to ___ up with her boyfriend after three years. (break)
items.explain: Break up with = end a relationship.

items.prompt: They want to ___ down and buy a house. (settle)
items.explain: Settle down = start a stable life.

items.prompt: I can't ___ up with his loud music any longer. (put)
The couple ___ up last month after five years together. (break up)
items.explain: Break up: broke up in the past.

items.prompt: We argued, but we ___ up the next morning. (make up)
items.explain: Make up: made up in the past.

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
items.explain: With a pronoun, put it between the verb and the particle.

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
'Drift apart' means...
items.explain: Drift apart is a slow change.

items.prompt: Which phrasal verb means 'tolerate'?
items.explain: Put up with = accept something annoying.

items.prompt: If you ___ touch with someone, you stop communicating.
'You can count on him' means...
I get along them well.
answers: I get along with them well.

items.prompt: He let down her.
items.explain: A pronoun goes before the particle.

items.prompt: I can't put up him.
answers: I can't put up with him.
items.explain: The verb is put up with.

items.prompt: We lost the touch after university.
Put the words in order.
answers: They broke up after two years together

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: I try to keep in touch with my cousins

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: Can I count on you to be there
items.explain: Count on someone to do something.

items.prompt: Me llevo muy bien con mis compañeros de trabajo.
answers: I get along very well with my coworkers.
I get along very well with my colleagues.
I get on very well with my coworkers.
I get on very well with my colleagues.

items.prompt: No soporto el ruido de mis vecinos.
answers: I can't put up with my neighbors' noise.
I can't put up with the noise from my neighbors.
I can't stand my neighbors' noise.
I can't stand the noise from my neighbors.

items.prompt: Quiero sentar cabeza algún día.
answers: I want to settle down someday.
I want to settle down one day.

sets.title: Both, neither, either, each other and softeners
sets.intro: Use both, neither and either to talk about two people or things. Softeners make your opinions sound polite.

watch.wrong: Neither of us don't like horror films.
watch.right: Neither of us likes horror films.
watch.why: Neither already has a negative meaning.

watch.wrong: They love each others.
watch.right: They love each other.

watch.wrong: She is both clever or funny.
watch.right: She is both clever and funny.

items.prompt: ___ of my parents speaks French.
items.explain: Neither + of + plural noun takes a singular verb.

items.prompt: We ___ work in finance.
items.explain: With a normal verb, both goes before it.

items.prompt: She is ___ funny and generous. (both ... and)
items.explain: Both ... and joins two similar ideas.

items.prompt: He is neither lazy ___ rude.
They have known ___ since primary school.
items.explain: Each other shows a two-way action.

items.prompt: I don't think ___ of them is telling the truth.
Both of ___ enjoy cooking.
The two friends help ___ with their homework.
Do you want tea or coffee? — ___ is fine; I don't mind.
items.explain: Either means one or the other, no preference.

items.prompt: It is ___ cold nor wet today, so let's walk.
The film is a ___ long, but I enjoyed it. (softener = slightly)
I wouldn't ___ he is rude, but he isn't exactly polite. (softener)
He talks a lot. He is very kind, ___. (softener at the end)
items.explain: Though at the end adds a contrast.

items.prompt: It is kind ___ weird that they never call.
Neither of the answers ___ correct.
items.explain: Neither already has a negative meaning.

items.prompt: Anna and Sofia don't see ___ often.
Which sentence is correct?
items.explain: Both of us takes a plural verb.

items.prompt: Which is the softest way to criticize?
We ___ live downtown.
items.explain: Both goes before a normal verb.

items.prompt: I don't like ___ of the two films.
items.explain: Either is used in negative sentences.

items.prompt: Neither of us don't like horror films.
answers: Neither of us likes horror films.
Neither of us like horror films.

items.prompt: We met each others at university.
answers: We met each other at university.

items.prompt: She is both clever or funny.
answers: She is both clever and funny.

items.prompt: Both of they are teachers.
items.explain: After of, use an object pronoun.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: Neither of my cousins lives nearby
items.explain: Neither of + plural noun + singular verb.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: They both work at the same hospital
items.explain: Both goes before a normal verb.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: It's a bit strange but I like it

items.prompt: Ninguno de los dos quiere ir.
answers: Neither of them wants to go.
Neither of them want to go.

items.prompt: Los dos son muy simpáticos.
answers: Both of them are very nice.
Both of them are very friendly.

items.prompt: Se escriben cada semana.
answers: They write to each other every week.
They write each other every week.
They write to one another every week.
items.explain: Each other = el uno al otro.

sets.title: Wishes and regrets: wish and if only
sets.intro: We use wish and if only to say that we want reality to be different. The verb moves one tense back.

watch.wrong: I wish I would be taller.
watch.right: I wish I were taller.
watch.why: Do not use would for your own situation.

watch.wrong: I wish I didn't go to that party.
watch.right: I wish I hadn't gone to that party.
watch.why: A past regret needs had + past participle.

watch.wrong: If only I would have known!
watch.right: If only I had known!
watch.why: Never use would have after wish or if only.

items.prompt: I wish I ___ more free time. (have)
items.explain: Wish + past simple = a wish about the present.

items.prompt: I wish I ___ less busy. (be)
items.explain: Use were (or was in speech) after wish.

items.prompt: If only he ___ here now! (be)
We wish we ___ afford a bigger flat.
items.explain: Wish + could = ability we don't have.

items.prompt: I wish you ___ stop interrupting me.
items.explain: Wish + would = annoying behavior we want to change.

items.prompt: I wish I ___ studied harder at school.
items.explain: Wish + past perfect = regret about the past.

items.prompt: If only we ___ argued last night.
She wishes she ___ gone to the concert, but she was ill.
items.explain: Wish + could have + participle = past ability.

items.prompt: I regret ___ him my password. (tell)
He wishes he ___ a car, but he can't afford one. (have)
I wish it ___ raining. (stop)
items.explain: Wish + would for something that annoys us.

items.prompt: If only I ___ the answer! (know)
I wish I ___ told her the truth.
They regret ___ the house so cheaply. (sell)
I wish I ___ taller.
items.explain: A present wish takes the past (were).

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I wish I would have more time.
I wish I had more time.
I wish I have more time.
I wish I will have more time.
items.explain: Wish is followed by a past form.

items.prompt: 'I wish I had called her' means...
items.explain: Past perfect after wish shows regret.

items.prompt: Which sentence is about annoying behavior?
options: I wish you would be quiet.
I wish you were quiet yesterday.
items.explain: Wish + would = we want someone to change.

items.prompt: If only we ___ the train!
I regret ___ to the party.
I wish I would be taller.
items.explain: Do not use would for yourself; use the past.

items.prompt: I wish I didn't buy that car.
answers: I wish I hadn't bought that car.
items.explain: A regret about the past needs the past perfect.

items.prompt: If only I would have more money.
answers: If only I had more money.
items.explain: Use the past simple, not would.

items.prompt: She wishes she can speak French.
answers: She wishes she could speak French.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: I wish I lived closer to my family

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: If only we had left earlier

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: He wishes he could play the piano

items.prompt: Ojalá tuviera más tiempo libre.
answers: I wish I had more free time.
If only I had more free time.

items.prompt: Ojalá no hubiera dicho eso.
answers: I wish I hadn't said that.
If only I hadn't said that.

items.prompt: Me arrepiento de no haber estudiado más.
answers: I regret not having studied more.
I wish I had studied more.
If only I had studied more.

sets.title: Third and mixed conditionals
sets.intro: The third conditional imagines a different past. A mixed conditional links a past event with a present result, or the opposite.

watch.wrong: If I would have known, I would have called.
watch.right: If I had known, I would have called.
watch.why: Never use would in the if clause.

watch.wrong: If she had studied, she would passed.
watch.right: If she had studied, she would have passed.
watch.why: After would, use have + past participle.

watch.wrong: If I had taken that job, I would have lived in Toronto now.
watch.right: If I had taken that job, I would be living in Toronto now.
watch.why: A present result needs would + base verb.

items.prompt: If I ___ known about the delay, I would have left earlier. (know)
If she hadn't missed the bus, she ___ have been late.
We would have won if we ___ the ball more. (pass)
If we had left earlier, we ___ have caught the train.
items.explain: The result clause takes would / could / might have.

items.prompt: What would you ___ done if you had lost your phone?
If I ___ studied medicine, I would be a doctor now. (have)
If I weren't so shy, I ___ have asked her out.
If he ___ taken that job, he would be rich now. (have)
If you hadn't forgotten the tickets, we ___ in the cinema now. (be)
items.explain: Mixed: would + base verb for the present result.

items.prompt: They ___ have been happier if they had moved to the coast.
If it ___ rained, the picnic would have been perfect. (not)
She wouldn't be tired today if she ___ to bed earlier last night. (go)
If I'd known, I'd ___ called you.
items.explain: The 'd in the result clause is would; then have + participle.

items.prompt: If I ___ more confident, I would have applied for the manager job. (be)
items.explain: Mixed: a present characteristic explains a past result.

items.prompt: If I ___ harder, I would have passed.
items.explain: The if clause uses had + participle.

items.prompt: Which is a mixed conditional?
options: If I had taken that job, I would be in Paris now.
If I had taken that job, I would have been in Paris.
If I take that job, I will be in Paris.
If I took that job, I would be in Paris.
items.explain: Past condition with a present result.

items.prompt: If she ___ the bus, she wouldn't have been late.
Which sentence is correct?
options: If I had known, I would have told you.
If I would have known, I would have told you.
If I knew, I would have told you.
If I had known, I would told you.
items.explain: Never use would have in the if clause.

items.prompt: If he ___ the keys, we wouldn't be standing outside now.
items.explain: A mixed conditional: past if clause, present result.

items.prompt: 'If I'd known' means...
If I would have known, I would have called.
answers: If I had known, I would have called.
items.explain: The if clause takes had + participle.

items.prompt: If she had studied, she would passed.
answers: If she had studied, she would have passed.
items.explain: Would is followed by have + participle.

items.prompt: If we had left earlier, we will have arrived on time.
answers: If we had left earlier, we would have arrived on time.
items.explain: Use would have, not will have, in the third conditional.

items.prompt: If I wouldn't be so tired, I would have gone out.
answers: If I weren't so tired, I would have gone out.
If I wasn't so tired, I would have gone out.
items.explain: No would in the if clause.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: If I had known I would have helped you

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: What would you have done if you had failed

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: If I had saved more I would be rich now

items.prompt: Si hubiera sabido, te habría llamado.
answers: If I had known, I would have called you.
items.explain: Si hubiera + participio = if + had + participle.

items.prompt: Si no hubiera llovido, habríamos ido a la playa.
answers: If it hadn't rained, we would have gone to the beach.
If it had not rained, we would have gone to the beach.

items.prompt: Si hubiera estudiado medicina, ahora sería doctor.
answers: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
If I had studied medicine, I'd be a doctor now.

sets.title: Advice, criticism and regret
sets.intro: Use if I were you, had better and should have to give advice, warn someone or criticize the past.

watch.wrong: If I was you, I will study more.
watch.right: If I were you, I would study more.
watch.why: Advice: if I were you + would.

watch.wrong: You had better to call him.
watch.right: You had better call him.
watch.why: Had better is followed by the base verb.

watch.wrong: You should told me.
watch.right: You should have told me.

items.prompt: If I ___ you, I'd take the scholarship.
items.explain: In advice, use were after if I.

items.prompt: You'd ___ call him before it's too late.
items.explain: You'd better + base verb is a strong warning.

items.prompt: You ___ have told me about the problem earlier. (criticism)
items.explain: Should have + participle criticizes a past action.

items.prompt: I ___ have said that. I'm really sorry.
You ___ have asked for help, but you didn't. (a missed option)
items.explain: Could have + participle = a possibility you didn't use.

items.prompt: You ___ have bought flowers. It wasn't necessary.
items.explain: Needn't have + participle = it was unnecessary.

items.prompt: You ___ want to visit the campus first. (soft advice)
items.explain: You might want to ... is gentle advice.

items.prompt: If I were you, I ___ talk to the manager.
You'd better ___ late for the interview. (negative)
items.explain: Negative: had better not + base verb.

items.prompt: I would ___ accept the offer. (almost 100% sure)
items.explain: In affirmative sentences the adverb follows would.

items.prompt: You ___ better take an umbrella. It's going to rain.
items.explain: Had better is followed by the base verb.

items.prompt: She ___ have called us; we were worried. (criticism)
We needn't ___ rushed; the train was late. (have)
Why ___ you ask your boss for a day off?
items.explain: Why don't you ...? is a friendly suggestion.

items.prompt: If I ___ you, I'd see a doctor.
items.explain: If I were you ... is the usual form.

items.prompt: Which sentence criticizes a past action?
options: You might want to call me.

items.prompt: 'You needn't have come' means...
options: It wasn't necessary to come, but you came.
items.explain: Needn't have = unnecessary action that happened.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest warning?
options: You might want to be on time.
items.explain: Had better not is a strong warning.

items.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
Where does the adverb go in a negative sentence?
If I were you, I will study more.
answers: If I were you, I would study more.

items.prompt: You had better to call him.
You should told me earlier.
answers: You should have told me earlier.

items.prompt: You needn't to have bought flowers.
items.explain: Needn't is followed by have, not to have.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: If I were you I would apologize
items.explain: Advice with if I were you.

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: You should have checked the schedule first

items.prompt: Put the words in order.
answers: You had better not touch that button
